Discussion of Ordinance Amendments 2 WHITE LAKE TOWNSHIP PLANNING COMMISSION OCTOBER 15, 2026 Item A. Planning Consultants David and Mateo, together with Township Attorney Deb, presented a draft data center zoning ordinance for Commission review in advance of a public hearing. The following topics were discussed, with staff directed to refine the draft accordingly. No formal motions or votes were taken on the ordinance itself; this remains a discussion item pending a public hearing. Overlay District and Location The Commission expressed general support for establishing a dedicated Data Center Overlay District (approximately 230 acres across roughly 18-20 parcels) in the northeast corner of the Township near the existing Mack Industries site, rather than permitting data centers as a special land use throughout the entire LM (Light Manufacturing) district. The rationale discussed included consistency with the Master Plan's future land use designation for industrial expansion in that area and a desire to limit data center siting to a defined, already industrially-oriented area. Setbacks Consensus leaned toward retaining a 300-foot setback measured from the property line of the applicable structure or equipment to residentially-zoned property lines, with acknowledgment that this figure could be increased (e.g., to 500 feet) if warranted. The Commission discussed using the setback as a supporting measure for noise, emissions, and visual massing concerns rather than as a standalone requirement. Noise and Vibration The draft ordinance's noise standards (45 dB residential standard, with a 6-decibel tonal penalty), vibration provisions, and infrasound concerns were discussed at length. The Commission was provided redlined additions from a sound and vibration consultant engaged by a neighboring township (Lion Township) for consideration prior to the public hearing. Staff noted that three acoustical consulting firms had been contacted; one indicated a baseline noise study would be required (at a cost of approximately 20,000 dollars) and declined to comment further, while responses from the other two were pending. Water Use and Natural Resources The draft ordinance's groundwater and surface water provisions (baseline groundwater assessment, monitoring, and contingency/mitigation plans) were reviewed. Discussion included whether to require closed-loop cooling systems rather than evaporative systems; several Commission members expressed support for requiring closed-loop systems, though no formal decision was made. It was clarified that water withdrawal and discharge approvals generally fall under the jurisdiction of Oakland County Health Department or the Michigan Department of Environment, Great Lakes, and Energy (EGLE), not the Township. Decommissioning The draft ordinance's decommissioning financial guarantee (currently set at 125% of estimated cost, reviewed and adjusted every 5 years for inflation) was discussed. A recommendation was made to increase the guarantee to 150%, consistent with standard practice referenced by a Commission member with real estate experience. Discussion also addressed clarifying that the Township select (rather than merely approve) the qualified professional preparing the decommissioning cost estimate, and that the Township retain the right to challenge the estimate. 3 WHITE LAKE TOWNSHIP PLANNING COMMISSION OCTOBER 15, 2026 Item A. Enforcement and Remedies The Commission discussed adding express authority for the Township to initiate legal proceedings to obtain compliance, in addition to existing remedies, within the operational compliance/escrow section of the ordinance. The Township Attorney indicated this language had been intended for inclusion and would be confirmed/added. Annual Reporting and Generators The Commission discussed whether annual third-party inspection/reporting requirements (and the associated funding escrow) should be specific to data centers or extended more broadly to any use exceeding a defined threshold of generators or electrical wattage, in order to avoid the appearance of singling out data centers. Consensus was to explore a broader, metric-based threshold (by generator count and/or wattage) for potential inclusion in the LM district standards or nuisance ordinance. Transfer of Ownership A Commission member raised concern that the draft's transfer-of-ownership provisions were vague regarding successor obligations. The Township Attorney agreed to review and clarify this section. Architectural Standards The draft ordinance's architectural review requirements for data center structures were discussed; no changes were proposed, though members noted the inconsistency with the lack of similar requirements for other LM district uses. Appeal Procedure It was clarified that provisions within the draft ordinance (including the operational compliance escrow section) would be appealable to the Zoning Board of Appeals (ZBA), consistent with other zoning ordinance provisions. Moratorium and Timeline Staff noted the Township's data center moratorium expires February 12, 2027, and has previously been extended once. The Commission discussed the possibility of deferring final action to a second November meeting, if needed, to allow additional review time while still meeting the moratorium deadline. NOW HEREBY the Charter Township of White Lake ordains the following amendments to the White Lake Charter Township Zoning Ordinance: PART 1: Article 2.0, Definitions, Section 2.2, Definitions Amend Article 2.0, Definitions, Section 2.2, Definitions, to add the following new definitions, to be inserted in alphabetical order among the existing definitions. All existing definitions in Section 2.2 shall remain unchanged and in full force and effect; this Part adds definitions only and does not amend, repeal, or replace any existing definition. The new definitions shall read as follows: A-Weighted Sound Level (dBA): The sound pressure level, expressed in decibels (dB), as measured using the A-weighting frequency network of a sound level meter conforming to American National Standards Institute (ANSI) standard S1.4 for sound level meters. A-weighting adjusts the measured sound pressure across the frequency spectrum to approximate the sensitivity of the human ear. Ambient Sound Level: The all-encompassing sound level associated with a given environment at a specified location and time, typically a composite of sound from many sources, near and far. Background Sound Level: The sound level that is present in a given environment at a specified location and time, in the absence of any identified intermittent or intrusive sound sources, typically characterized by the sound level exceeded 90 percent of the measurement period (L90). Battery Energy Storage System (BESS): One or more devices, assemblies, or containers capable of storing electrical energy for later use through electrochemical technologies, including associated control systems, inverters, transformers, cooling systems, fire-suppression equipment, and related infrastructure. C-Weighted Sound Level (dBC): The sound pressure level, expressed in decibels (dB), as measured using the C-weighting frequency network of a sound level meter conforming to American National Standards Institute (ANSI) standard S1.4 for sound level meters. C-weighting applies little or no adjustment across most of the audible frequency spectrum, and includes lowfrequency energy typically down to 10 or 12.5 Hz, below the normally recognized range of human hearing. C-weighting is commonly used to assess low-frequency noise content. Data Center: A facility or group of buildings whose primary function is the housing, operation, and maintenance of computer servers, data-storage systems, telecommunications equipment, and associated infrastructure used for the processing, storage, or transmission of digital 8 Zoning Ordinance Amendment- 26-003, as presented to the Planning Commission for the December 3, 2026 public hearing Item A. information. Such facilities may include backup power generation, cooling systems, fuel storage, Battery Energy Storage Systems, substations, and security infrastructure. This term does not include a server room or data-processing facility that is accessory, incidental to and housed entirely within a permitted principal use, and requires no additional approvals from a utility provider with respect to electrical or water usage. Data Center Campus: The entire Data Center development subject to a common Special Land Use approval and Concept Master Development Plan, whether consisting of one Data Center building or multiple buildings, located on one parcel or multiple contiguous or functionally integrated parcels, and whether constructed at one time or in phases. For purposes of Section 4.61, every Data Center shall be reviewed as a Data Center Campus. Decibel (dB): A unit of measurement, on a logarithmic scale, used to express the magnitude of sound pressure relative to a standard reference pressure of 20 micropascals (20 µPa), the threshold of human hearing. Emergency: An unforeseen occurrence or condition requiring immediate action to protect life, health, safety, property, or essential utility service, including an actual utility power outage requiring operation of backup electrical power. Emergency does not include routine testing, scheduled maintenance, planned load management, peak shaving, demand-response participation, elective grid-support operation, or other planned or discretionary operation. Equivalent Continuous Sound Level (Leq): A sound level obtained from energy averaging over a specified time interval. This level is obtained using an integrating averaging sound level meter, which determines the mean of the square of the sound pressure over a specified time interval, and expresses the result in decibels. The level is designated as Leq, along with the time period of measurement, i.e. 50 dBA Leq-1hr. Impulsive Sound: Sound of short duration, usually less than one second, with an abrupt onset and rapid decay. Examples of sources of impulsive sound include explosions, drop forge impacts, and discharge of firearms. L90 Sound Level: A statistical sound level quantity representing the sound level exceeded 90% of the measurement period. The L90 sound level is commonly used to measure the background sound level of a given environment. Legal Holiday: The following legal public holidays: New Year's Day (January 1); Memorial Day (last Monday in May); Independence Day (July 4); Labor Day (first Monday in September); Thanksgiving Day (fourth Thursday in November); Christmas Eve Day (December 24); and Christmas Day (December 25). The Consolidated Plan is carried out through Annual Action Plans, which provide a concise summary of the actions, activities, and the specific federal resources that will be used each year to address the priority needs and specific goals identified by the Consolidated Plan. The applicant is requesting a rezoning of the 1.48-acre property at 525 N Pennsylvania Avenue from “R-MX” Mixed Residential to “R-AR” Residential Adaptive Reuse and a special land use permit to allow a sheltered care facility within the existing building. According to the applicant and the online sale listing the property has been used for medium-intensity congregation space and offices. The intent of the R-MX Mixed Residential district is to accommodate a mixture of housing types along corridors, particularly near the downtown. Historically, these areas were single-family neighborhoods that have transitioned over time to include a mixture of housing types ranging from middle-housing types (two-to-six dwelling units) to moderate walk-up multi-family dwellings. R-MX designation for the property is most similar to the previous zoning ordinance designation of DM-3, Multiple Family Residential. Shelters are essential to the community and should primarily be located in close proximity to the downtown and to hospitals where they can effectively serve the majority of the population in need of their services. The subject property is in an area that is just outside the fringe of the downtown but within walking distance thereof and is on a major bus route that provides transportation throughout the City. The purpose of requiring a special land use permit is so that each proposal can be evaluated to determine if a particular site is appropriate for use as a shelter and will not negatively impact other uses in the surrounding area. COMPATIBILITY WITH SURROUNDING LAND USES Historically the subject property has been used to provide community services for those in need as well as a child day care program, and worship services, none of which have been disruptive to other uses in the area. The surrounding neighborhood is unique in that there are residential uses of varying densities including single-family homes, duplexes, middle housing (up to 6 units) and multi-family apartments. There are a few vacant properties resulting from demolitions in the area. In addition, the area includes large industrial and office uses, light commercial establishments and the UM-Health Sparrow’s main hospital campus. The unhoused population in Lansing has grown in recent years and there is a need to provide additional shelter space. Since a shelter will intensify the use of the subject property, particularly during evening hours, it is important to limit any potential negative impacts on the adjoining residential neighborhood. Public hearings shall be conducted during the New Business portion of the meeting as follows: 1. Explanation of the request as received by the Commission. 2. Review and recommendations by the Commission staff and consultants. 3. Comments and explanations by applicant. 4. Questions by the Commission. 5. Responses by Liaisons, consultants, and/or the applicant. 6. Opening of hearing for public comments. 7. Closing of hearing to public comments. 8. The Chair may call upon the Liaisons, consultants, and/or the applicant to respond to questions or make additional comments. 9. Consideration of action by the Commission. PUBLIC PARTICIPATION 1. All public comment should be presented during the time(s) designated on the agenda. Public comment is normally not allowed outside of those times; however, sometimes the Commission may recognize members of the public to speak. 2. Public comment at all Commission meetings shall be conducted according to the following rules: a. The Chair opens the meeting for public comment and summarizes the rules of conduct for public comments as outlined in this section. For public hearings, the Chair will also announce the topic under consideration. b. All public speakers are encouraged to identify themselves by full name and community of residence prior to speaking. c. All comments must be addressed to the Chair. d. Speakers are given only three minutes each. Speakers are not permitted to grant their time to an alternate speaker. During public hearings, public comment and discussion shall be limited to the topic under consideration. e. Each person will be given an opportunity to be heard. After every person interested in addressing the Commission has spoken, the Chair may permit additional public comments. f. The Chair may limit the amount of time allowed for each person wishing to make public comment at a Commission meeting. The Chair may ask members of the audience to caucus with others sharing similar positions so they may select a single spokesperson. If a single spokesperson is selected, that individual shall be able to make public comment at the Commission meeting without time limit or an extended time limit. DISORDERLY CONDUCT AT MEETINGS 1. Members of the public shall not interrupt Commission members, Liaisons, or individuals permitted to address the Commission while they are speaking during a meeting or otherwise disrupt a Commission meeting. 2. The Chair may call to order any attendee who: a. Engages in personal attacks which disrupt the meeting, incite violence or raise issues that are unrelated to Commission business; b. Uses obscene or grossly indecent language; c. Speaks longer than the allotted time; d. Disrupts the proceedings; e. Otherwise violates the rules of the Commission. 3. Failure to come to order may result in the forfeiture of any remaining speaking time, or, at the request of the Chair, expulsion from the meeting.

RESOLUTION #261101 TYRONE TOWNSHIP, LIVINGSTON COUNTY AMENDMENT OF ARTICLE 21 OF THE TYRONE TOWNSHIP ZONING ORDINANCE SUPPLEMENTAL DISTRICT REGULATIONS TYRONE TOWNSHIP REGULAR BOARD MEETING APPROVED MINUTES – NOVEMBER 17, 2026 – PAGE 2 An Ordinance to amend the Tyrone Township Zoning Ordinance to update Township regulations governing medical marijuana caregivers in accordance with the provisions of state law, MCL 125.3101 et seq. and MCL 333.26421 et seq. THE TOWNSHIP OF TYRONE LIVINGSTON COUNTY, MICHIGAN ORDAINS AS FOLLOWS: Section 1 of Ordinance Article 21, Section 21.55 of the Tyrone Township Zoning Ordinance shall be amended by replacing the entirety of current language of Article 21, Section 21.55 with the following: SECTION 21.55 MEDICAL MARIJUANA CAREGIVER OPERATIONS A. Purpose. It is the purpose of this Section to impose specific requirements for any facility where those individuals registering with the State of Michigan as a “qualifying patient” or a “primary caregiver,” as those terms are defined in the Michigan Medical Marihuana Act, Initiated Law 1 of 2008, MCL 333.26421 et seq., as amended, conduct activity related to the authorized medical use of marijuana in the Township so as to protect the health, safety and welfare of the general public. Tyrone Township is not legalizing or permitting the use of controlled substances within its borders, whether that substance is medical marijuana or any other identified as a controlled substance. Rather, Tyrone Township is establishing locations and regulations for uses set forth in the Act to comply with the Act. If after adoption, any portion of the Act is repealed, or any portion of the Act is deemed unconstitutional by the Michigan Supreme Court or a lower Michigan court decision chosen not to be heard by the Michigan Supreme Court, any activities or uses within this Ordinance applicable to the repealed or unconstitutional portion of the Act are immediately repealed as well. At the time of adoption, the Michigan Supreme Court and Michigan Attorney General had ruled or opined collectives, dispensaries, or cooperative establishments existing to allow primary caregivers or qualifying patients to share or transfer medical marijuana between primary caregivers or between qualifying patients, or which allow contact with or access to medical marijuana by those not registered with the State of Michigan as primary caregivers or qualifying patients, are not permitted by the Act. It is further intended that nothing in this Section be construed to allow persons to engage in conduct that endangers others or causes a public nuisance, or to allow use, possession or control of marijuana for nonmedical purposes or allow activity relating to cultivation/growing, distribution or consumption of marijuana that is otherwise illegal under State law. B. Definitions. For purposes of this section, the words and phrases contained herein shall have the meanings set forth in the Michigan Medical Marihuana Act, Initiated Law 1 of 2008, MCL 333.26421 et seq., as amended (hereafter referred to in this section as “the Act”) and the regulations adopted by the State of Michigan, Department of Community Health, pursuant to authority conferred by Section 5 of the Act, inclusive of all amendments to the Act. For the purposes of this Ordinance, the terms “marijuana” and “marihuana” as used here, in the Act, and elsewhere, shall be synonymous. TYRONE TOWNSHIP REGULAR BOARD MEETING APPROVED MINUTES – NOVEMBER 17, 2026 – PAGE 3 1. Department of Licensing and Regulatory Affairs or LARA means the State of Michigan Department of Licensing and Regulatory Affairs cited in the Act and responsible for the registration of primary caregivers and qualifying patients. This term shall also refer to any successor department, agency or bureau that is subsequently assigned the duties and responsibilities specified in the Act. 2. Marijuana, also known as Marihuana, also known as Cannabis has the meaning given to it in Section 7601 of the Michigan Public Health Code, 1978 PA 368, MCL 333.7106. 3. Medical Marijuana Caregiver Operation or Caregiver Operation means any parcel, lot or facility where a registered primary caregiver cultivates, manufactures, extracts, distributes, or possesses marijuana, marijuana infused products or paraphernalia for a qualifying patient to whom they are connected through LARA’s registration process for medical use. The term “caregiver operation” shall not include the private cultivation, manufacture, extraction or possession of marijuana for medical use by a registered qualifying patient in compliance with the restrictions of the Act. 4. Medical Use of Marijuana means the acquisition, possession, cultivation, manufacture, extraction, use, internal possession, delivery, transfer, or transportation of marijuana, marijuana-infused products, or paraphernalia relating to the administration of marijuana to treat or alleviate a registered qualifying patient's debilitating medical condition or symptoms associated with the debilitating medical condition. 5. Primary Caregiver or Registered Primary Caregiver is defined as set forth in the Act. 6. Qualifying Patient or Registered Qualifying Patient is defined as set forth in the Act. C. Permitted Uses. A caregiver operation shall only be conducted under the following standards: 1. The primary caregiver shall only cultivate, manufacture, extract, possess or transfer marijuana, marijuana-infused products or paraphernalia for medical use for no more than five (5) qualifying patients to whom they are connected through LARA’s registration process. 2. Only one (1) primary caregiver shall operate within and/or upon the caregiver operation parcel, lot or facility. D. Prohibited Uses and/or Activities. explicitly prohibited. Any use which is not specifically listed in Sec. 21.55.C is E. Location Where permitted. A caregiver operation shall comply with the following location requirements: 1. Permitted Districts. Caregiver operations shall only be located in the B-2, M-1 or M-2 zoning districts. 2. Separation from other operations. Caregiver operations shall not be directly adjacent to another parcel or lot where a caregiver operation has been approved to operate. TYRONE TOWNSHIP REGULAR BOARD MEETING APPROVED MINUTES – NOVEMBER 17, 2026 – PAGE 4 3. Residential Setback. Caregiver operations, including all buildings and enclosed locked facilities, shall be located at least 500 feet from any residentially used, zoned or planned parcel or lot. The setback distance shall be measured from the nearest point on the caregiver operation’s property line shared and directly adjacent to the residentially used, zoned or planned parcel or lot to the closest point of any caregiver operation building or enclosed locked facility. 4. School and Child Care Setback. Caregiver operations, including all buildings and enclosed locked facilities, shall be located at least 500 feet from the nearest lot line of any child care center, licensed day care facility, preschool program center, primary, intermediate or secondary school, or like facility, established pursuant to and in accordance with the Revised School Code, P.A. 451 of 1976, being M.C.L.A. §§ 380.1 through 380.1853, as amended, and/or the State School Aid Act of 1979, P.A. 94 of 1979, being M.C.L.A. §§ 388.1601 through 388.1772, as amended. Measurement of the 500 foot setback shall be made from the outermost property line boundaries of the lot or parcel upon which the caregiver operation will be situated to the nearest point on a property line of the lot or parcel which the buffered use is located. F. Property Control. The site for a caregiver operation must be under the control, through written lease, contract, or deed, in favor of the primary caregiver or a registered qualifying patient associated with that facility to whom the primary caregiver is connected through LARA’s registration process. G. Enclosed Locked Facility. For each registered qualifying patient to whom a primary caregiver is connected through LARA’s registration process and who has specified that the primary caregiver will be allowed under state law to cultivate marijuana for the qualifying patient, no more than twelve (12) marijuana plants shall be kept in an enclosed locked facility at the caregiver operation. An enclosed locked facility means: 1. For marijuana grown indoors, a closet, room, or other comparable, stationary, and fully enclosed area equipped with secured locks or other functioning security devices that permit access only by the registered primary caregiver or registered qualifying patient associated with that facility. 2. For marijuana grown outdoors: a. An area that is not visible to the unaided eye from an adjacent property when viewed by an individual standing at ground level or from a permanent structure; and b. Plants are grown in a stationary structure that is enclosed on all sides, except for the base, by six foot high chain link fencing, wooden slats, or similar fencing/wall material that prevents access by the general public and that is anchored, attached or affixed to the ground; and c. Located on land that is owned, leased, or rented by either a registered primary caregiver or the registered qualifying patient for whom the marijuana plants are grown; and d. Equipped with functioning locks and other security devices that restrict access to only the associated qualifying patient or caregiver. e. The required fencing or wall shall be of new, high quality material, shall meet all County and Township Code requirements, and is subject to Township inspection at any time to insure that it remains in proper and functioning condition. TYRONE TOWNSHIP REGULAR BOARD MEETING APPROVED MINUTES – NOVEMBER 17, 2026 – PAGE 5 H. Lighting. If a room with windows is utilized as a growing location, any lighting between 10:00 PM and 7:00 AM shall be shielded to prevent ambient light spillage onto adjacent residential properties. I. Signage. A primary caregiver operation shall not have any signage. J. Wastewater. The site and caregiver operation shall be designed and operated so as to minimize the amount of pesticides, fertilizers, nutrients, marijuana, and any other potential contaminants discharged into the public wastewater and/or stormwater systems. The applicant shall provide a list of all chemicals used on site including, but not limited to, all cleaners, solvents, nutrients and any other product used to clean, treat and grow the facility and products created on site. Any proposed site intending to utilize a septic field system for wastewater treatment shall provide a report from the County Health Department indicating that a medical marijuana grow operation and all associated chemicals and nutrients will be in compliance with all applicable health codes, rules and statutes. K. Odor. Caregiver operations which grow marijuana within a building shall be equipped with an operable filtration, ventilation, and exhaust system that effectively confines odors to the interior of the building from which the odor is generated. Caregiver operations which grow marijuana outdoors shall be required to locate the marijuana such that no odor is discernable at any property line. L. Security. Caregiver operations shall be designed to comply with the requirements for an enclosed, locked facility and shall consistently maintain this standard to effectively prohibit unauthorized access. Caregiver operations shall be available for inspection by any authorized law enforcement officer or State inspector to confirm the operation is operating in accordance with State laws and the Township Supervisor or their designee, to confirm the operation is operating in accordance with Township zoning ordinances. M. Site Plan Application and Review. Caregiver operations shall be required to apply for site plan approval in compliance with Article 23. At the time of application for site plan review, the primary caregiver must provide a copy of their valid primary caregiver registration. The applicant must consent to verification through LARA of the number of registered qualifying patients associated with the primary caregiver and receiving services from the primary caregiver. Section 2 of Ordinance With the exception of the amendment of Article 21, Section 21.55 in the manner specified above, the Township Zoning Ordinance shall remain in full force and effect. Section 3 of Ordinance This ordinance amendment shall be effective on the date provided by law following publication, subject to the provisions of the Michigan Zoning Enabling Act.
